q: A four-top books your tasting menu and one guest is not drinking. Design her experience and defend the pricing.
accept: build the same arc out of acid tannin bitterness and savoury depth
teas verjus shrubs and dashi served in the same glassware at the same moment
avoid sweetness fatigue and structure the flight like a wine flight
price it below the wine pairing but not free because the labour is higher
ans: She gets a pairing, not an apology. I build the same arc the wine flight builds — aperitif, lighter courses, a substantial one, a sweet close — out of things with real structure. Chilled dashi or clarified tomato water where I need savoury depth; verjus or a good non-alcoholic sparkling for lift and acid; cold-brewed teas used as varietals, gyokuro for umami, hojicha for roast, a lapsang against anything charred; a shrub or kombucha where I want tannic grip; a bitter aromatic build with tonic where I would otherwise have poured something phenolic. What every glass must supply is acid, tannin or bitterness, temperature contrast and a savoury note. Sweetness is what makes these programmes fail: sugar across nine courses exhausts a palate faster than alcohol does. Service is the other half of it — same glassware, poured at the same moment, announced with the same detail, so nobody at the table is watching one person be accommodated. On price I charge, usually somewhat below the wine flight because the raw cost is lower, but never nothing, because the labour is higher: these are made in-house, they do not keep, and the reason the category was bad for a generation is that nobody was paid to make it good.
exp: The competency is structural, not encyclopedic: a candidate who lists trendy products but cannot say what each one is doing to the palate has missed it. Two things to flag if the examiner pushes. Dealcoholised wine is usually the weakest item available, because stripping the alcohol strips the aromatics it carried. And the hospitality point outranks the liquid — a guest who is not drinking notices being served differently long before she notices what is in the glass.

q: Two hundred covers, a plated dinner, three wines. Plan the operation, with your numbers.
accept: a bottle is twenty five ounces so five pours at five ounces means forty bottles per wine
open taste and stage everything before doors and sample cases for taint
calculate bottles per wine then add ten to fifteen per cent cushion
stage the whites into ice in waves and hold the reds at cellar temperature
~forty bottles per wine
~40 bottles per wine
~ten to fifteen per cent over
~five ounce pour gives five glasses
ans: Start from the arithmetic. A 750 ml bottle is 25.4 ounces, so a five-ounce pour gives five glasses and a four-ounce pour gives six. If every guest takes one glass of each wine that is forty bottles per wine at five ounces, and I order ten to fifteen per cent over — call it forty-five each, a hundred and thirty-five bottles — with reception sparkling costed separately at roughly a bottle for every four to five guests through the first hour. Then the physical plan. Everything is opened, sniffed and staged before doors, because there is no recovery from finding a corked bottle at table nineteen while two hundred plates leave the pass; sample across the cases on arrival. Temperature is the part that actually goes wrong at volume: whites into ice in waves rather than all at once, or they reach the guest at three degrees tasting of nothing, and reds off the delivery early, held at cellar temperature and never parked near the kitchen. Staff around one pourer to every sixteen to twenty covers, plus runners on wine only, each with a fixed section so no table is poured twice and none is missed. Pour on the course, not ahead of it, from the guest's right. Brief the whole floor before service with two sentences on each wine so any one of them can answer a question without fetching me. Afterwards I count what came back unopened — that number tells me whether I planned the night or guessed it.
exp: Banquet questions are graded on arithmetic and on failure modes. The arithmetic is one line — 25.4 ounces per bottle — and every quantity follows from it. The failure modes are almost never quantity: they are temperature and pre-opening, because both are invisible until the wine is in front of a guest and neither can be fixed once two hundred plates are moving. Counting the unopened bottles at the end is what turns one banquet into a forecast for the next.

q: The KWV's historical role and its dismantling date:
accept: cooperative quota control ended 1990s 1997
statutory coop set quotas prices ended 1997
ans: The statutory co-op fixed quotas, prices and distillation minimums (1918–1997); its end unleashed the modern industry
exp: Post-1994 politics and post-KWV economics are one story.

q: Explain the Cape's brandy tradition and its legal standard.
accept: potstill brandy 30 percent minimum copper double distilled three years
cape brandy potstill
ans: Cape Potstill Brandy: double-distilled in copper pot stills, matured at least 3 years in small (≤340 L) oak; blended South African brandy must contain a minimum of 30% potstill brandy
exp: Historically the Cape's largest spirit output, now a quality niche.

mullineux porseleinberg sadie
ans: Mullineux, Porseleinberg, Sadie, Boekenhoutskloof — dry-farmed old bush vines on schist and granite, whole-bunch, restrained alcohol, savoury rather than jammy
exp: The Cape's strongest claim to a red style of its own.

q: Trace Sémillon's rise and fall in the Cape: what it was called, how much of the vineyard it held, and where its old vines survive.
accept: groendruif green grape about ninety percent of cape plantings now around one percent
dominant in the nineteenth century now under two percent
franschhoek old vines and semillon gris survive
called groendruif nearly all cape vines then collapsed
ans: In the early nineteenth century Sémillon effectively was the Cape vineyard — contemporary counts put it near ninety per cent of plantings. It was known as groendruif, 'green grape', or simply wyndruif, the wine grape, because it needed no other name. Phylloxera, the turn to higher-yielding whites, and then the KWV's distilling-driven economy reduced it to around one per cent today. The survivors carry the story: century-old blocks in Franschhoek, the Landau du Val vines of 1905 among them, and the field mutation Sémillon Gris, whose pink-skinned vines are scattered through those same old rows and are now bottled on their own.
exp: Master answers reward a variety's arc, not its flavour. Sémillon is the Cape's best evidence that its vineyard is a rebuilt one, and Sémillon Gris is the kind of detail that separates a candidate who has walked Franschhoek's old blocks from one who has read a textbook.

q: Name Stellenbosch's registered wards and characterise three of them.
accept: bottelary devon valley papegaaiberg polkadraai hills jonkershoek banghoek simonsberg-stellenbosch
simonsberg-stellenbosch jonkershoek valley banghoek polkadraai bottelary
seven wards including simonsberg-stellenbosch and jonkershoek valley
banghoek bottelary devon valley papegaaiberg polkadraai
ans: The long-established wards are Bottelary, Devon Valley, Papegaaiberg, Polkadraai Hills, Jonkershoek Valley, Banghoek and Simonsberg-Stellenbosch, with further wards registered since. Simonsberg-Stellenbosch: north-eastern, decomposed-granite slopes facing the mountain, the district's Cabernet and Pinotage heartland — Kanonkop, Rustenberg, Thelema. Jonkershoek Valley: a narrow, steep, cool amphitheatre with high rainfall and late ripening, giving structured Cabernet from Neil Ellis and Stark-Condé. Polkadraai Hills: south-west, the closest to False Bay and the most wind-cooled, now the source of the district's finest Sauvignon and Chenin. Bottelary lies on sandy granitic hills with old bush-vine Pinotage and Cinsaut; Devon Valley is a small clay-rich bowl; Papegaaiberg is the tiny hill at the town's edge.
exp: Stellenbosch is not one place, and a Master candidate is expected to break it apart aloud — granite versus shale, mountain versus bay, and which producer proves each point. Anchoring each ward to an aspect, a soil and a name is the difference between recitation and argument.

q: Speak to water in the Cape: the 2015–2018 drought, what it cost, and how the vineyard is answering.
accept: day zero drought 2018 harvest down about fifteen percent and shrinking vineyard area
2015 to 2018 western cape drought and day zero
dryland bush vines and drought tolerant rootstocks are the answer
vineyard area has fallen below 90000 hectares
ans: Three failed winters emptied the Western Cape's dams and brought Cape Town to the brink of 'Day Zero' in early 2018. The 2018 crop came in roughly fifteen per cent below the previous year, and the irrigated bulk areas along the Breede and Olifants — where water is the yield — suffered worst, while dryland bush vines in the Swartland were comparatively unmoved. National vineyard area has fallen from over 100,000 hectares in the mid-2000s to under 90,000 today; drought, unsustainably low grape prices and leafroll together. The answers are dryland bush-vine viticulture, which the Swartland never abandoned; moving quality plantings to cooler, wetter, higher and more coastal sites; drought-tolerant rootstocks such as Richter 110 and 99; canopy and cover-crop management to hold soil moisture; and precise deficit irrigation where water exists at all.
exp: Climate questions at Master level want consequence and response, not weather. The Cape's contraction in hectares is the single most important structural fact about the industry right now, and drought is only one of its three causes — say all three.
